text: David Gruber wants to know what sperm whales are saying. He thinks it might actually be possible. Photo by Michael Lees / National Geographic Society Gruber is a marine biologist, a professor, and the founder of Project CETI , the Cetacean Translation Initiative, a project using artificial intelligence and machine learning to decode the communication of sperm whales. To some, it’s the most audacious scientific undertaking of our time. To others, a beautiful fool’s errand. Gruber sees it as the next logical step. He started, as many scientists do, as a kid who couldn’t stop staring. Growing up in New Jersey, Gruber was the boy crouched in the grass, watching ants, not with the detached curiosity of a future entomologist, but with something closer to kinship. He was a sensitive, awkward child who connected more easily with the small creatures in his backyard than with other kids. That quality never left him. It became his method.
